claims.text: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can exist as a disordered random BCC solid solution.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has high configurational entropy.
Atomic-size mismatch produces significant lattice distortion in random HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal annealing or controlled cooling can induce chemical short-range order in HfNbTaTiZr.
Ordering in HfNbTaTiZr preferentially forms HfTi and TiZr binary clusters.
The HfTi and TiZr clusters can develop B2-like order and form a percolating network while the alloy remains single-phase BCC.
There is a temperature window that activates diffusion for SRO formation while remaining below the phase-separation temperature.
B2-like clusters locally regularize the atomic environment and reduce the variance of local size and elastic properties relative to the random alloy.
The transition from random disorder to B2-like SRO reduces RMS atomic displacement and local lattice strain.
Mass and atomic-size fluctuations in random alloys strongly scatter high-frequency phonons.
Reducing static lattice disorder increases high-frequency phonon group velocity and lifetime.
Percolation of low-distortion ordered regions creates continuous pathways for enhanced heat transport.
Enhanced transport through the percolating ordered network outweighs phonon scattering at chemical-ordering boundaries.
SRO formation produces a net increase in lattice thermal conductivity relative to random HfNbTaTiZr.
SRO formation hardens the high-frequency phonon DOS, shifting its peak to higher frequencies.
Ordered clusters have lower atomic-displacement amplitudes and Debye-Waller factors than the random alloy.
A conductivity increase requires the ordered clusters to percolate and reduce average lattice distortion without secondary-phase precipitation or macroscopic phase separation.
Large incoherent precipitates or macroscopic phase separation introduce sufficient interface scattering to produce a conductivity decrease.

contradictions.description: The boundary permits lower conductivity when annealing causes phase separation or incoherent precipitates, but the falsification rule treats any lower conductivity in the annealed sample as falsifying the mechanism without first requiring confirmation that the sample remained single-phase and within the stated boundary conditions.
